newsitem.title: KYRGYZSTAN: Kyrgyz leader says concerned over NATO expansion.
newsitem.headline: Kyrgyz leader says concerned over NATO expansion.

text.p: Kyrgyz President Askar Akayev said during a visit by NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana on Wednesday that he shared Russian worries over the Western defence alliance's plans to expand eastwards.
"We share Russian concerns about NATO enlargement," Akayev told a news conference in Bishkek, capital of the mountainous former Soviet republic.
"Russia is our strategic partner," Akayev said. "I want to find a common language between NATO and Russia."

Solana is on a five-day tour of four Central Asian nations in an attempt to convince these ex-Soviet states that NATO's sparring with the Kremlin over its planned eastward enlargement does not threaten stability in their own countries.

Moscow and NATO are at loggerheads over the alliance's intention to offer membership invitations at a summit in Madrid in July. Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are favourites to be the first new entrants.
Akayev echoed concerns expressed by Kazakh Foreign Minister Kasymzhomart Tokayev on Tuesday.
"The process of expansion is inevitable but it is important to heed Russia's concerns," Tokayev said during Solana's visit to Kazakhstan.
Thousands of kilometres (miles) east of Europe, Western diplomats say the remote mountains, desert and steppe of Central Asia are a long way from NATO's main sphere of interest.
The Central Asian republics themselves remain dependent on Moscow, particularly for energy exports, and are careful to preserve good relations with their former colonial master.
Solana is officially touring Central Asia to discuss the participation of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan in NATO's "Partnership for Peace" programme.

He promised NATO aid for a fledgling peacekeeping battalion comprising troops from Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. The three states will hold a joint 10-day peacekeeping exercise with NATO in the region in September.
Solana's visit to other former Soviet republics in February prompted strong words from a suspicious Kremlin.

Solana and the Central Asian republics have been at pains to stress NATO involvement in anything from fighting drug trafficking to environmental protection and have kept away from sensitive defence issues.
"NATO has changed significantly, with the organisation's main target now peacekeeping duties," Solana said in a speech to the Kyrgyz parliament.

Solana was due to go to the Uzbek capital of Tashkent late on Wednesday where he can expect a warmer welcome. Uzbek President Islam Karimov, keen for strong ties with the United States, has said he has no problems with NATO expansion eastwards.
